{{< include /_includes/mm-setup.qmd >}}

This appendix is for readers who met vectors, derivatives and standard deviations once, in a first-year course, and have not touched them since: chemists, biologists and anyone whose maths is rusty. If you have a mathematics or physics degree, skip it; nothing here will be new. Nothing here is required reading *before* the episodes either. Each section opens with the episodes that use the idea, so you can come back when a formula or a line of NumPy stops you, read the one section you need, and return.

Every section is built the same way. First the theory: the definitions, stated precisely, and the results the episodes rely on, with a short proof where a proof is genuinely illuminating and a sketch or a reference where it is not. Then the same ideas in a few small NumPy cells that make them concrete. The cells run top to bottom, so copy any of them into a notebook and change the numbers. Each section ends with ★ self-checks and hidden solutions.

Definitions, theorems and propositions are numbered in order of appearance on this page. Proofs are collapsed; open them when you want to see *why* a statement holds, not just that it does.

```{python}
import numpy as np
import pandas as pd

penguins = pd.read_csv("data/penguins.csv").dropna()
columns = ["bill_length_mm", "bill_depth_mm", "flipper_length_mm", "body_mass_g"]
```

## Notation

| Symbol | Meaning |
|---|---|
| $\mathbb{R}$, $\mathbb{R}^n$, $\mathbb{R}^{m \times n}$ | the real numbers; vectors with $n$ real entries; matrices with $m$ rows and $n$ columns |
| $x_i$, $A_{ij}$ | entry $i$ of the vector $x$; the entry of the matrix $A$ in row $i$, column $j$ |
| $x^\top$, $A^\top$ | transpose: a column vector written as a row; rows and columns of $A$ swapped |
| $\operatorname{span}$, $\dim$, $\operatorname{rank}$ | the span of some vectors; the dimension of a space; the rank of a matrix |
| $\operatorname{col}(A)$, $\operatorname{null}(A)$ | column space and null space of a matrix |
| $\lVert x \rVert$, $\lVert x \rVert_1$ | Euclidean norm (length) of $x$; the $\ell_1$ norm $\sum_i \lvert x_i \rvert$ |
| $\sum_{i=1}^{n} x_i$ | the sum $x_1 + x_2 + \cdots + x_n$; the limits are omitted when they are clear |
| $f'(x)$, $\partial L / \partial \theta_j$, $\nabla L$ | derivative; partial derivative; gradient (the vector of all partial derivatives) |
| $\Omega$, $P(A)$, $P(A \mid B)$ | sample space; probability of the event $A$; probability of $A$ given $B$ |
| $F_X$, $p_X$, $f_X$ | distribution function, probability mass function and density of a random variable $X$ |
| $\mathbb{E}[X]$, $\operatorname{Var}(X)$, $\operatorname{Cov}(X, Y)$ | expectation, variance and covariance |
| $X \sim N(\mu, \sigma^2)$, $\Phi$ | "$X$ has the normal distribution with mean $\mu$ and variance $\sigma^2$"; the standard normal distribution function |
| $\bar{x}$, $s^2$ | sample mean and sample variance of a list of numbers |
| $\hat{y}$, $\hat{\theta}$ | a prediction, an estimate; the hat marks a quantity computed from data |
| $\arg\min_\theta L(\theta)$ | the value of $\theta$ at which $L$ is smallest |

Lower-case letters ($x$, $w$, $\theta$, $\lambda$) are vectors or scalars, and the text always says which; in this course a vector is a column by default, so $x^\top w$ is a number and $x w^\top$ is a matrix. Upper-case letters are matrices in the linear-algebra sections and random variables in the probability sections; the context always decides. Chapter 2 writes the intercept of a linear model as $\theta_0$ and the feature weights as $\theta_1, \ldots, \theta_p$; this appendix writes a general parameter vector as $\theta = (\theta_1, \ldots, \theta_p)^\top$.

## Vectors and vector spaces

*Used in* [episode 1.2](../part-1-foundations/ch01-scientific-python/02-numpy-arrays.html) (arrays), [episode 2.2](../part-1-foundations/ch02-ml-fundamentals/02-linear-regression.html) (the linear model, and why duplicated features break it) and [episode 2.4](../part-1-foundations/ch02-ml-fundamentals/04-overfitting-regularisation.html) (the norms behind ridge and lasso).

The vector you will meet most often in this course is the description of one sample: the four measurements of one penguin, or the handful of descriptors of one molecule. Each position in the list is one {{< term feature >}}, and the order never changes, so position 3 always means "flipper length". In NumPy a vector is a one-dimensional {{< term ndarray >}}.

```{python}
penguin = penguins[columns].iloc[0].to_numpy()  # bill length, bill depth, flipper length (mm), body mass (g)
penguin, penguin.shape
```

The {{< term shape >}} `(4,)` says: one axis, four entries. What makes such lists useful is not the numbers themselves but two operations, adding two of them and scaling one by a number, and the rules those operations obey. The same rules hold for many other objects (spectra, functions, matrices), so mathematics states them once.

::: {.definition title="Vector space"}
A (real) **vector space** is a set $V$ together with an addition, which gives $u + v \in V$ for $u, v \in V$, and a scalar multiplication, which gives $\lambda v \in V$ for $\lambda \in \mathbb{R}$ and $v \in V$, such that for all $u, v, w \in V$ and all $\lambda, \mu \in \mathbb{R}$:

1. $u + v = v + u$ and $(u + v) + w = u + (v + w)$;
2. there is a **zero vector** $0 \in V$ with $v + 0 = v$, and every $v$ has a **negative** $-v \in V$ with $v + (-v) = 0$;
3. $\lambda (u + v) = \lambda u + \lambda v$, $(\lambda + \mu) v = \lambda v + \mu v$ and $\lambda (\mu v) = (\lambda \mu) v$;
4. $1\, v = v$.

The elements of $V$ are called **vectors** and the real numbers $\lambda$ **scalars**.
:::

The basic example is $\mathbb{R}^n$, the lists of $n$ real numbers, with addition and scaling done entry by entry; the space of penguin feature vectors is $\mathbb{R}^4$. Matrices of a fixed shape form a vector space in the same way, and so do real-valued functions, with $(f + g)(x) = f(x) + g(x)$: every prediction function of a model is a vector in that sense. A non-example is instructive: the set of concentration vectors, whose entries are non-negative, is *not* a vector space, because $(1, 2)$ belongs to it and $-1 \cdot (1, 2)$ does not.

```{python}
p1, p2 = penguins[columns].iloc[:2].to_numpy()
p1 + p2, 0.5 * (p1 + p2)  # the average of two penguins is again a vector in R^4
```

::: {.definition title="Subspace"}
A **subspace** of a vector space $V$ is a subset $U \subseteq V$ that is itself a vector space with the same addition and scalar multiplication.
:::

::: {.proposition title="Subspace test"}
A subset $U \subseteq V$ is a subspace if and only if $0 \in U$ and $U$ is closed under both operations: $u + v \in U$ and $\lambda u \in U$ for all $u, v \in U$ and $\lambda \in \mathbb{R}$.
:::

::: {.proof}
First two consequences of the axioms. $0\,v = (0 + 0)\,v = 0\,v + 0\,v$, and adding $-(0\,v)$ to both sides gives $0\,v = 0$. Then $v + (-1)v = (1 - 1)v = 0\,v = 0$, so $(-1)v = -v$.

If $U$ is a subspace, it is closed under the operations by definition, and its zero vector $0_U$ satisfies $0_U + 0_U = 0_U$; adding $-0_U$ (in $V$) to both sides gives $0_U = 0$, so $0 \in U$. Conversely, if $U$ contains $0$ and is closed, the operations of $V$ are operations on $U$; every axiom holds in $U$ because it holds in $V$, the zero vector is in $U$ by assumption, and the negative of $u \in U$ is $(-1)u \in U$.
:::

### Linear combinations, independence and bases

::: {.definition title="Linear combination and span"}
A **linear combination** of vectors $v_1, \ldots, v_k \in V$ is a vector $\lambda_1 v_1 + \cdots + \lambda_k v_k$ with scalars $\lambda_1, \ldots, \lambda_k$. The **span** of $v_1, \ldots, v_k$ is the set of all their linear combinations; by the subspace test it is a subspace, and it is the smallest subspace containing all the $v_i$.
:::

::: {.definition title="Linear independence"}
Vectors $v_1, \ldots, v_k$ are **linearly independent** if the only scalars with $\lambda_1 v_1 + \cdots + \lambda_k v_k = 0$ are $\lambda_1 = \cdots = \lambda_k = 0$. Otherwise they are **linearly dependent**; then at least one of them is a linear combination of the others (solve the equation for any $v_j$ whose coefficient is non-zero).
:::

::: {.definition title="Basis and dimension"}
A **basis** of $V$ is a list $b_1, \ldots, b_n$ of linearly independent vectors that spans $V$. If $V$ has a basis with $n$ elements, $V$ has **dimension** $n$, written $\dim V = n$.
:::

::: {.theorem title="Bases and coordinates"}
Let $V$ be a vector space with a basis $b_1, \ldots, b_n$.

1. Every $v \in V$ can be written as $v = c_1 b_1 + \cdots + c_n b_n$ in exactly one way; the numbers $c_1, \ldots, c_n$ are the **coordinates** of $v$ in that basis.
2. Every basis of $V$ has exactly $n$ elements, so the dimension is well defined, and any $n$ linearly independent vectors in $V$ form a basis.
3. In $\mathbb{R}^n$ the **standard basis** $e_1, \ldots, e_n$, where $e_j$ has a 1 in position $j$ and zeros elsewhere, is a basis; so $\dim \mathbb{R}^n = n$, and the coordinates of $x$ in the standard basis are its entries.
:::

::: {.proof}
Item 1: a representation exists because the basis spans $V$. If $v = \sum_i c_i b_i = \sum_i d_i b_i$, then $\sum_i (c_i - d_i) b_i = 0$, and linear independence forces $c_i = d_i$ for every $i$. Item 3: $x = \sum_j x_j e_j$ shows that the $e_j$ span $\mathbb{R}^n$, and $\sum_j \lambda_j e_j = (\lambda_1, \ldots, \lambda_n)$ is zero only if every $\lambda_j$ is. Item 2 rests on the *exchange lemma*: in a space spanned by $n$ vectors, any linearly independent list has at most $n$ elements. Applied in both directions to two bases it shows they have the same length; its proof is in any linear-algebra text and is not needed here.
:::

In data terms, the *columns* of a feature matrix are vectors too: one entry per sample. If one feature is a linear combination of others, for instance the same mass recorded in grams and in kilograms, or a total that is the sum of its parts, the columns are linearly dependent and carry less information than their number suggests. NumPy's `matrix_rank` (defined properly in the next section) counts how many columns are independent.

```{python}
X4 = penguins[columns].to_numpy()
X5 = np.column_stack([X4, penguins["body_mass_g"].to_numpy() / 1000])  # the same mass again, in kg
X4.shape, np.linalg.matrix_rank(X4), X5.shape, np.linalg.matrix_rank(X5)
```

Five columns, but only four independent ones: the kilogram column is $1/1000$ times the gram column. The coefficients that show the dependence form a non-zero vector $v$ with $X_5 v = 0$:

```{python}
v_dep = np.array([0, 0, 0, 1, -1000])  # 1 x (mass in g) - 1000 x (mass in kg)
np.abs(X5 @ v_dep).max()  # zero, up to floating-point rounding
```

::: {.challenge level=1 title="Which are subspaces?"}
Which of these subsets of $\mathbb{R}^3$ are subspaces? (a) $\{x : x_1 + x_2 + x_3 = 0\}$; (b) $\{x : x_1 = 1\}$; (c) $\{x : x_1 \ge 0\}$; (d) the span of $(1, 0, 0)$ and $(0, 1, 0)$.

:::: {.solution}
Use the subspace test. (a) Yes: it contains $0$, and if two vectors have entries summing to zero, so do their sum and every multiple. (b) No: it does not contain $0$. (c) No: $(1, 0, 0)$ is in it but $-1 \cdot (1, 0, 0)$ is not, so it is not closed under scalar multiplication. (d) Yes: a span is always a subspace; this one is the plane $x_3 = 0$, of dimension 2.
::::
:::

::: {.challenge level=2 title="A hidden dependence"}
A descriptor table for five hypothetical molecules has three columns: the number of carbon atoms, the number of other heavy atoms, and the total number of heavy atoms. Are the columns linearly independent? Find a non-zero vector $v$ with $Xv = 0$, and say what that means for a linear model fitted on all three columns.

:::: {.solution}
The total is the sum of the other two, so the columns are dependent and $v = (1, 1, -1)$ gives $Xv = 0$ for every row, whatever the molecules are.

```{python}
counts = np.array([[6, 1], [2, 1], [7, 2], [10, 4], [3, 0]])  # carbon, other heavy atoms (made-up rows)
Xh = np.column_stack([counts, counts.sum(axis=1)])
np.linalg.matrix_rank(Xh), Xh @ np.array([1, 1, -1])
```

For a linear model this means the weights are not determined: adding any multiple of $v$ to a weight vector changes no prediction, because $X(\theta + t v) = X\theta$. The least-squares theorem in the derivatives section shows that the fit then has infinitely many solutions, which is one of the reasons regularisation exists ([episode 2.4](../part-1-foundations/ch02-ml-fundamentals/04-overfitting-regularisation.html)). Note that the dependence must be *linear*: a column holding the ratio of the first two would not lower the rank.
::::
:::

## Matrices and linear maps

*Used in* [episode 1.2](../part-1-foundations/ch01-scientific-python/02-numpy-arrays.html) and [episode 2.2](../part-1-foundations/ch02-ml-fundamentals/02-linear-regression.html) (the linear model and the normal equation).

::: {.definition title="Matrix and transpose"}
A **matrix** $A \in \mathbb{R}^{m \times n}$ is a rectangular array of real numbers with $m$ rows and $n$ columns; its entry in row $i$ and column $j$ is $A_{ij}$. The pair $(m, n)$ is its **shape**. The **transpose** $A^\top \in \mathbb{R}^{n \times m}$ is the matrix with $(A^\top)_{ij} = A_{ji}$: rows become columns.
:::

Stack the feature vectors of several samples as rows and you get the matrix that every scikit-learn model expects: one row per sample, one column per feature. This is the {{< term xy-convention >}}, and it is worth fixing in your head now because every `.fit(X, y)` in the course relies on it.

```{python}
X = penguins[columns].head(3).to_numpy()
X
```

```{python}
X.shape, X.T.shape
```

Shape is always `(rows, columns)`, that is `(n_samples, n_features)`. `X[0]` is the first penguin's feature vector; `X[:, 3]` is the body mass of every penguin; the transpose `X.T` has one row per feature and one column per penguin.

### Products

::: {.definition title="Matrix–vector and matrix–matrix products"}
For $A \in \mathbb{R}^{m \times n}$ and $w \in \mathbb{R}^n$, the product $Aw \in \mathbb{R}^m$ has entries
$$
(Aw)_i = \sum_{j=1}^{n} A_{ij}\, w_j .
$$
For $A \in \mathbb{R}^{m \times k}$ and $B \in \mathbb{R}^{k \times n}$, the product $AB \in \mathbb{R}^{m \times n}$ has entries
$$
(AB)_{ij} = \sum_{l=1}^{k} A_{il}\, B_{lj} .
$$
The products are defined only when the inner dimensions agree: $n$ in the first case, $k$ in the second.
:::

::: {.proposition title="Rules for products"}
Let $A$, $B$, $C$ be matrices whose shapes make the products below defined. Then

1. $(m \times k)$ times $(k \times n)$ has shape $(m \times n)$: inner dimensions must match, outer dimensions remain;
2. $(AB)C = A(BC)$ and $A(B + C) = AB + AC$;
3. $(AB)^\top = B^\top A^\top$;
4. in general $AB \neq BA$, and one side may not even be defined.
:::

::: {.proof}
Items 1 and 4 are immediate from the definition. Item 2 is a reindexing of finite sums. For item 3, by the definitions of transpose and product,
$$
\big((AB)^\top\big)_{ij} = (AB)_{ji} = \sum_l A_{jl} B_{li} = \sum_l (B^\top)_{il} (A^\top)_{lj} = (B^\top A^\top)_{ij} .
$$
:::

Another way to read $Aw$: it is the linear combination of the *columns* of $A$ with coefficients $w_1, \ldots, w_n$. Row by row it is one dot product per row (dot products are the subject of the next section): the sum of each feature times its weight for sample $i$. A linear model predicts exactly this way, $\hat{y} = X w$, so `X @ w` is `LinearRegression.predict` in one line, up to the intercept that `predict` adds.

```{python}
w = np.array([0.1, -0.2, 0.05, 0.001])
X @ w
```

```{python}
np.sum(X[0] * w)  # the first entry, done by hand
```

The shapes must agree: `(3, 4) @ (4,)` gives `(3,)`. If the number of weights does not match the number of columns, NumPy refuses, which is a useful error to see early. The matrix product you will see in [episode 2.2](../part-1-foundations/ch02-ml-fundamentals/02-linear-regression.html) is $X^\top X$, which by item 1 is square with one row and column per feature, and by item 3 is its own transpose.

```{python}
(X.T @ X).shape
```

::: {.pitfall title="`*` is not matrix multiplication"}
In NumPy `X * w` multiplies element by element (and broadcasts `w` across the rows); `X @ w` is the matrix product. Both run without error on the arrays above, and only one of them is what the linear model does. If a hand calculation disagrees with your code, check which operator you used.
:::

### Linear maps

::: {.definition title="Linear map"}
A function $T : V \to W$ between vector spaces is **linear** if $T(u + v) = T(u) + T(v)$ and $T(\lambda v) = \lambda\, T(v)$ for all vectors $u, v$ and scalars $\lambda$.
:::

::: {.proposition title="Matrices are linear maps"}
For every $A \in \mathbb{R}^{m \times n}$ the map $x \mapsto Ax$ from $\mathbb{R}^n$ to $\mathbb{R}^m$ is linear. Conversely, every linear map $T : \mathbb{R}^n \to \mathbb{R}^m$ is of this form, with the matrix whose $j$-th column is $T(e_j)$. Composing linear maps corresponds to multiplying their matrices: $x \mapsto A(Bx)$ is $x \mapsto (AB)x$.
:::

::: {.proof}
Linearity of $x \mapsto Ax$ is item 2 of the rules for products. Conversely, write $x = \sum_j x_j e_j$; linearity gives $T(x) = \sum_j x_j\, T(e_j)$, which is the matrix with columns $T(e_j)$ applied to $x$. The last statement is associativity, $A(Bx) = (AB)x$.
:::

```{python}
x_a, x_b = np.array([1.0, 0.0, 2.0, 0.5]), np.array([0.0, 3.0, -1.0, 1.0])
np.allclose(X @ (2 * x_a + x_b), 2 * (X @ x_a) + X @ x_b)  # linearity, checked numerically
```

### Column space, null space and rank

::: {.definition title="Column space, null space, rank"}
For $A \in \mathbb{R}^{m \times n}$, the **column space** $\operatorname{col}(A) = \{Ax : x \in \mathbb{R}^n\} \subseteq \mathbb{R}^m$ is the span of the columns of $A$, and the **null space** $\operatorname{null}(A) = \{x \in \mathbb{R}^n : Ax = 0\}$ is the set of vectors $A$ sends to zero. Both are subspaces. The **rank** of $A$ is $\operatorname{rank}(A) = \dim \operatorname{col}(A)$, the largest number of linearly independent columns.
:::

::: {.theorem title="Rank–nullity"}
For every $A \in \mathbb{R}^{m \times n}$,
$$
\operatorname{rank}(A) + \dim \operatorname{null}(A) = n .
$$
Moreover $\operatorname{rank}(A) = \operatorname{rank}(A^\top)$, so $\operatorname{rank}(A) \le \min(m, n)$.
:::

::: {.proof}
A sketch of the first statement. Choose a basis $u_1, \ldots, u_k$ of $\operatorname{null}(A)$ and extend it (by the exchange lemma) to a basis $u_1, \ldots, u_k, w_1, \ldots, w_r$ of $\mathbb{R}^n$, so $k + r = n$. Every $Ax$ is a combination of the $Aw_i$, because the $Au_i$ are zero; and the $Aw_i$ are independent, because $A(\sum_i c_i w_i) = 0$ puts $\sum_i c_i w_i$ in the null space, which forces every $c_i$ to be zero. So $\operatorname{rank}(A) = r = n - k$. The equality of row rank and column rank is a standard theorem that we use without proof.
:::

The theorem turns into a statement about data. A feature matrix with $p$ columns and rank $r$ has a null space of dimension $p - r$: that many independent directions in which the weights of a linear model can move without changing a single prediction. With more features than samples ($p > n$), the rank is at most $n < p$, so such directions always exist. The kilogram column above is a one-dimensional example.

::: {.proposition title="The matrix XᵀX"}
For every $X \in \mathbb{R}^{n \times p}$, $\operatorname{null}(X^\top X) = \operatorname{null}(X)$. Consequently $X^\top X$ is invertible if and only if the columns of $X$ are linearly independent.
:::

::: {.proof}
If $Xv = 0$ then $X^\top X v = 0$. Conversely, if $X^\top X v = 0$ then $0 = v^\top X^\top X v = (Xv)^\top (Xv) = \lVert Xv \rVert^2$, so $Xv = 0$. The second statement combines this with the theorem on linear systems below (an $n \times n$ matrix is invertible exactly when its null space is $\{0\}$) and the fact that $Xv = \sum_j v_j\, x_{\cdot j}$ is a combination of the columns $x_{\cdot j}$, so $\operatorname{null}(X) = \{0\}$ says precisely that the columns are independent.
:::

### Identity, inverse, and why we `solve`

::: {.definition title="Identity and inverse"}
The **identity matrix** $I_n \in \mathbb{R}^{n \times n}$ has ones on the diagonal and zeros elsewhere, so that $I_n v = v$ for every $v \in \mathbb{R}^n$. A square matrix $A \in \mathbb{R}^{n \times n}$ is **invertible** if there is a matrix $A^{-1}$ with $A^{-1} A = A A^{-1} = I_n$; $A^{-1}$ is then unique and is called the **inverse** of $A$.
:::

::: {.theorem title="Solving a linear system"}
Let $A \in \mathbb{R}^{n \times n}$. The following are equivalent:

1. $A$ is invertible;
2. for every $b \in \mathbb{R}^n$ the equation $A\theta = b$ has exactly one solution, namely $\theta = A^{-1} b$;
3. the only solution of $A\theta = 0$ is $\theta = 0$, that is $\operatorname{null}(A) = \{0\}$, that is the columns of $A$ are linearly independent.
:::

::: {.proof}
(1 ⇒ 2) If $A\theta = b$ then multiplying on the left by $A^{-1}$ gives $\theta = A^{-1} b$, so there is at most one solution; and $A(A^{-1} b) = b$, so there is at least one. (2 ⇒ 3) Take $b = 0$: the unique solution is $0$. (3 ⇒ 1) The $n$ columns of $A$ are independent, so by the theorem on bases they form a basis of $\mathbb{R}^n$ and span it. Hence each $e_j = A b_j$ for some $b_j$; the matrix $B$ with columns $b_j$ satisfies $AB = I_n$. Moreover $A(BA - I_n) = (AB)A - A = 0$, so every column of $BA - I_n$ solves $A\theta = 0$ and is zero by item 3; hence $BA = I_n$ as well, and $B = A^{-1}$.
:::

The theorem is why the {{< term normal-equation >}} of linear regression is usually *written* as $\theta = (X^\top X)^{-1} X^\top y$. It is not how it is *computed*. Forming an inverse explicitly is slower and loses precision, so numerical code asks NumPy to solve the equation directly: `np.linalg.solve(A, b)` returns the $\theta$ that satisfies $A\theta = b$ without ever building $A^{-1}$.

```{python}
A = np.array([[2.0, 1.0], [1.0, 3.0]])
b = np.array([3.0, 5.0])
theta = np.linalg.solve(A, b)
theta, A @ theta  # the second value should be b again
```

The check `A @ theta` returning `b` is the whole story: `solve` found the $\theta$ that makes the equation true. scikit-learn's `LinearRegression` uses a least-squares solver that also copes with dependent columns, but the idea is the same.

::: {.challenge level=1 title="Read the shapes"}
A feature matrix has 200 samples and 5 features. What are the shapes of `X`, `X.T`, `X @ w` (for a weight vector `w` with one weight per feature) and `X.T @ X`? What is the largest rank `X` can have?

:::: {.solution}
`X` is `(200, 5)`; `X.T` is `(5, 200)`; `X @ w` is `(200,)`, one prediction per sample; `X.T @ X` is `(5, 200) @ (200, 5)`, so `(5, 5)`, one row and column per feature. The rule is item 1 of the rules for products: inner dimensions must match, outer dimensions remain. By rank–nullity the rank is at most $\min(200, 5) = 5$, reached exactly when the five columns are linearly independent.
::::
:::

::: {.challenge level=1 title="One dot product per row"}
Without running code, compute `M @ v` for `M = [[1, 2], [3, 4], [5, 6]]` and `v = [10, 1]`. Then check with NumPy.

:::: {.solution}
Row by row: $1 \times 10 + 2 \times 1 = 12$, $3 \times 10 + 4 \times 1 = 34$, $5 \times 10 + 6 \times 1 = 56$. Equivalently, $10$ times the first column plus $1$ times the second.

```{python}
M = np.array([[1, 2], [3, 4], [5, 6]])
v = np.array([10, 1])
M @ v
```

Each output entry is the dot product of one row of `M` with `v`, which is why the result has one entry per row (shape `(3,)`).
::::
:::

## Inner products, norms and distances

*Used in* [episode 2.4](../part-1-foundations/ch02-ml-fundamentals/04-overfitting-regularisation.html) (the penalties of ridge and lasso), [episode 2.5](../part-1-foundations/ch02-ml-fundamentals/05-classification.html) (nearest neighbours) and [episode 2.6](../part-1-foundations/ch02-ml-fundamentals/06-pipelines-leakage.html) (feature scaling).

::: {.definition title="Dot product, Euclidean norm, distance"}
For $a, b \in \mathbb{R}^n$ the **dot product** (or standard inner product) is
$$
a \cdot b = \sum_{i=1}^{n} a_i b_i = a^\top b ,
$$
the **Euclidean norm** (length) of $a$ is $\lVert a \rVert = \sqrt{a \cdot a} = \sqrt{\sum_i a_i^2}$, and the **Euclidean distance** between $a$ and $b$ is $d(a, b) = \lVert a - b \rVert$.
:::

::: {.proposition title="Elementary properties"}
For all $a, b, c \in \mathbb{R}^n$ and scalars $\lambda$: $a \cdot b = b \cdot a$; $(\lambda a + c) \cdot b = \lambda (a \cdot b) + c \cdot b$; $\lVert \lambda a \rVert = |\lambda| \, \lVert a \rVert$; and $\lVert a \rVert \ge 0$ with equality only when $a = 0$.
:::

All four follow directly from the definition as a sum, and they are used silently in every argument below. The result that gives the dot product its geometric meaning is the following inequality.

::: {.theorem title="Cauchy–Schwarz inequality"}
For all $a, b \in \mathbb{R}^n$,
$$
|a \cdot b| \le \lVert a \rVert \, \lVert b \rVert ,
$$
with equality if and only if one of the vectors is a scalar multiple of the other.
:::

::: {.proof}
If $b = 0$ both sides are zero. Otherwise, for every real $t$ the squared length $\lVert a - t b \rVert^2$ is non-negative, and expanding it with the elementary properties gives
$$
0 \le \lVert a - t b \rVert^2 = \lVert a \rVert^2 - 2t\,(a \cdot b) + t^2 \lVert b \rVert^2 .
$$
Choose $t = (a \cdot b) / \lVert b \rVert^2$, the value that makes the right-hand side smallest. Then $0 \le \lVert a \rVert^2 - (a \cdot b)^2 / \lVert b \rVert^2$, which rearranges to the inequality. Equality holds exactly when $\lVert a - t b \rVert = 0$, that is when $a = t b$.
:::

::: {.definition title="Angle, cosine similarity, orthogonality"}
For non-zero $a, b$, the **cosine similarity** is $\cos\varphi = \dfrac{a \cdot b}{\lVert a \rVert \, \lVert b \rVert}$. By the Cauchy–Schwarz inequality it lies in $[-1, 1]$, so it is the cosine of a unique **angle** $\varphi \in [0, \pi]$ between the two vectors. Vectors with $a \cdot b = 0$ are **orthogonal**, written $a \perp b$.
:::

::: {.proposition title="Pythagoras and orthogonal projection"}
1. If $a \perp b$ then $\lVert a + b \rVert^2 = \lVert a \rVert^2 + \lVert b \rVert^2$.
2. Let $b \neq 0$. The vector $p = \dfrac{a \cdot b}{\lVert b \rVert^2}\, b$ is the only multiple of $b$ with $(a - p) \perp b$, and it is the point of the line through $b$ closest to $a$: $\lVert a - t b \rVert \ge \lVert a - p \rVert$ for every real $t$, with equality only at $p$. It is called the **orthogonal projection** of $a$ onto the line through $b$.
:::

::: {.proof}
Item 1: expand $\lVert a + b \rVert^2 = \lVert a \rVert^2 + 2\, a \cdot b + \lVert b \rVert^2$ and use $a \cdot b = 0$. Item 2: $(a - s b) \cdot b = a \cdot b - s \lVert b \rVert^2$ is zero exactly for $s = (a \cdot b) / \lVert b \rVert^2$, which gives $p$. For any $t$, $a - t b = (a - p) + (p - t b)$, and $p - tb$ is a multiple of $b$, hence orthogonal to $a - p$; by item 1, $\lVert a - t b \rVert^2 = \lVert a - p \rVert^2 + \lVert p - t b \rVert^2 \ge \lVert a - p \rVert^2$, with equality only when $tb = p$.
:::

Written as a sum, the dot product looks like bookkeeping. The theorem and the definition make it geometry: $a \cdot b = \lVert a \rVert \, \lVert b \rVert \cos\varphi$, so the dot product measures how much two vectors point the same way.

```{python}
a = np.array([3.0, 4.0])
b = np.array([4.0, 3.0])
a @ b, np.sum(a * b)  # the same number two ways
```

The norm is Pythagoras in as many dimensions as you like, and NumPy computes it with `np.linalg.norm`.

```{python}
np.linalg.norm(a), np.sqrt(a @ a)
```

Divide the dot product by both lengths and you are left with $\cos\varphi$: $1$ when the vectors point the same way, $0$ when they are perpendicular, $-1$ when they are opposite. For $a = (3, 4)$ and $b = (4, 3)$ the angle is small.

```{python}
cos_phi = (a @ b) / (np.linalg.norm(a) * np.linalg.norm(b))
cos_phi, np.degrees(np.arccos(cos_phi))
```

The projection of $a$ onto the line through $b$, and a check that what is left over is orthogonal to $b$:

```{python}
p = (a @ b) / (b @ b) * b
p, (a - p) @ b  # the second number is zero up to rounding
```

The number $a \cdot b / \lVert b \rVert$ is the signed length of that projection, the shadow $a$ casts on the line through $b$. So `X @ w` computes, for every row $x_i$, the shadow length of $x_i$ on the direction of $w$, multiplied by $\lVert w \rVert$: a linear model scores each sample by how far it extends along one direction in feature space. Cosine similarity comes back when you compare molecular fingerprints in Part II.

### Norms in general

::: {.definition title="Norm"}
A **norm** on a vector space $V$ is a function $v \mapsto \lVert v \rVert$ with, for all $u, v \in V$ and scalars $\lambda$:

1. $\lVert v \rVert \ge 0$, with equality only for $v = 0$;
2. $\lVert \lambda v \rVert = |\lambda| \, \lVert v \rVert$;
3. $\lVert u + v \rVert \le \lVert u \rVert + \lVert v \rVert$ (the **triangle inequality**).
:::

::: {.proposition title="Two norms on ℝⁿ"}
The Euclidean norm $\lVert x \rVert = \sqrt{\sum_i x_i^2}$ and the $\ell_1$ norm $\lVert x \rVert_1 = \sum_i |x_i|$ are both norms on $\mathbb{R}^n$. Consequently the Euclidean distance satisfies $d(x, z) \le d(x, y) + d(y, z)$ for all $x, y, z$.
:::

::: {.proof}
Items 1 and 2 are immediate for both. For the triangle inequality of the Euclidean norm, $\lVert a + b \rVert^2 = \lVert a \rVert^2 + 2\, a \cdot b + \lVert b \rVert^2 \le \lVert a \rVert^2 + 2 \lVert a \rVert \lVert b \rVert + \lVert b \rVert^2 = (\lVert a \rVert + \lVert b \rVert)^2$ by Cauchy–Schwarz. For $\ell_1$ it follows from $|a_i + b_i| \le |a_i| + |b_i|$ summed over $i$. For the distance, apply the triangle inequality to $a = x - y$ and $b = y - z$.
:::

The two norms measure size differently, and that is the whole difference between the two regularised regressions of [episode 2.4](../part-1-foundations/ch02-ml-fundamentals/04-overfitting-regularisation.html): ridge penalises $\alpha \lVert \theta \rVert^2$, the squared Euclidean norm of the weights, which shrinks all of them smoothly; lasso penalises $\alpha \lVert \theta \rVert_1$, which can set some exactly to zero.

```{python}
r = np.array([3.0, -4.0])
np.linalg.norm(r), np.linalg.norm(r, 1), np.abs(r).sum()
```

### Distance between two samples

```{python}
np.linalg.norm(a - b)
```

The Euclidean distance is what {{< term knn >}} uses to decide which training samples are "nearest" to a new one, and it is where units come in. Take one penguin of each species and compute the three pairwise distances on the raw measurements.

```{python}
three = penguins.groupby("species").head(1)
three[["species"] + columns]
```

```{python}
P = three[columns].to_numpy()
raw = np.array([[np.linalg.norm(p - q) for q in P] for p in P])
pd.DataFrame(raw, index=three["species"], columns=three["species"]).round(0)
```

The distances are 250, 750 and 1000: almost exactly the differences in body mass in grams. The bills differ by a few millimetres and the flippers by a few tens, and those numbers are tiny next to hundreds of grams, so they contribute nothing. Distance on raw features is a body-mass ranking in disguise.

{{< term feature-scaling >}} fixes this by putting every feature on the same footing. Standardise each column (subtract its mean, divide by its standard deviation; see [the statistics section](#mean-variance-and-distributions)) and compute the distances again.

```{python}
Z = (penguins[columns] - penguins[columns].mean()) / penguins[columns].std()
Pz = Z.loc[three.index].to_numpy()
scaled = np.array([[np.linalg.norm(p - q) for q in Pz] for p in Pz])
pd.DataFrame(scaled, index=three["species"], columns=three["species"]).round(2)
```

Now all four measurements count, and the answer changes: on raw numbers the Gentoo's nearest neighbour was the Adelie (750 g apart); after scaling it is the Chinstrap. The Chinstrap's bill is almost exactly as long as the Gentoo's (46.5 against 46.1 mm) and its flippers are closer (192 against 211 mm, where the Adelie has 181), and those millimetre differences finally count once the grams no longer swamp them. A kNN classifier would have flipped its vote. This is why scaling is part of the model, not a cosmetic step, and why [episode 2.6](../part-1-foundations/ch02-ml-fundamentals/06-pipelines-leakage.html) puts it inside a pipeline fitted on the training set only.

::: {.challenge level=1 title="Dot product and distance by hand"}
For $a = (1, 2, 2)$ and $b = (2, 0, 0)$, compute $a \cdot b$, $\lVert a \rVert$, $\lVert b \rVert$, $\cos\varphi$, the projection of $a$ onto the line through $b$, and the Euclidean distance $d(a, b)$. Then check with NumPy.

:::: {.solution}
$a \cdot b = 2 + 0 + 0 = 2$; $\lVert a \rVert = \sqrt{1 + 4 + 4} = 3$; $\lVert b \rVert = 2$; $\cos\varphi = 2 / (3 \times 2) = 1/3$; the projection is $(2/4)\, b = (1, 0, 0)$; $d(a, b) = \sqrt{(1-2)^2 + 2^2 + 2^2} = \sqrt{9} = 3$.

```{python}
a3 = np.array([1.0, 2.0, 2.0])
b3 = np.array([2.0, 0.0, 0.0])
a3 @ b3, np.linalg.norm(a3), np.linalg.norm(b3), (a3 @ b3) / (b3 @ b3) * b3, np.linalg.norm(a3 - b3)
```

A cosine of $1/3$ means the vectors point in broadly different directions (about 71°). Scaling a vector by a positive factor changes distances but not angles: $(2, 4, 4)$ makes the same angle with $b$ as $(1, 2, 2)$ does. A negative factor turns the angle $\varphi$ into $\pi - \varphi$.
::::
:::

::: {.challenge level=2 title="Where Cauchy–Schwarz bites"}
Suppose someone reports a cosine similarity of $1.04$ between two molecular fingerprints. Without seeing the fingerprints, what can you say? And if two non-zero vectors have cosine similarity exactly $-1$, what is the relationship between them?

:::: {.solution}
A cosine similarity above $1$ is impossible: by the Cauchy–Schwarz inequality $|a \cdot b| \le \lVert a \rVert \lVert b \rVert$, so the ratio lies in $[-1, 1]$. The number is a bug (most often a dot product divided by the wrong norms, or norms computed on different vectors). A cosine of exactly $-1$ is the equality case with a negative constant: $a = \lambda b$ with $\lambda < 0$, so the vectors point in exactly opposite directions.
::::
:::

## Derivatives and gradients

*Used in* [episode 2.2](../part-1-foundations/ch02-ml-fundamentals/02-linear-regression.html) (fitting by gradient descent) and every neural network from Chapter 4 on.

::: {.definition title="Derivative"}
A function $f : \mathbb{R} \to \mathbb{R}$ is **differentiable** at $x$ if the limit
$$
f'(x) = \lim_{h \to 0} \frac{f(x + h) - f(x)}{h}
$$
exists; $f'(x)$ is the **derivative** of $f$ at $x$. Geometrically it is the slope of the tangent line to the graph of $f$ at $x$; physically it is the rate at which $f$ changes per unit change in $x$.
:::

::: {.proposition title="Rules of differentiation"}
Where the functions involved are differentiable:

1. power rule: $\dfrac{d}{dx} x^k = k x^{k-1}$ for every real $k$ (and $x > 0$ when $k$ is not an integer);
2. linearity: $\dfrac{d}{dx}\big(c\, g(x) + u(x)\big) = c\, g'(x) + u'(x)$ for every constant $c$;
3. product rule: $\dfrac{d}{dx}\big(g(x)\, u(x)\big) = g'(x)\, u(x) + g(x)\, u'(x)$.
:::

::: {.theorem title="Chain rule"}
If $g$ is differentiable at $x$ and $f$ is differentiable at $g(x)$, then $f \circ g$ is differentiable at $x$ and
$$
\frac{d}{dx} f\big(g(x)\big) = f'\big(g(x)\big)\, g'(x) :
$$
the outer derivative, evaluated at the inner value, times the inner derivative.
:::

The chain rule is the one that matters for machine learning, because a loss is always "a function of the prediction, which is a function of the parameters". Its proof is in any calculus text; the idea is that for small $h$, $g(x + h) \approx g(x) + g'(x) h$, and then $f$ of that is approximately $f(g(x)) + f'(g(x))\, g'(x)\, h$.

The definition is also a way to *check* a derivative numerically. Pick a small $h$ and compute the ratio; the symmetric version $(f(x+h) - f(x-h)) / 2h$ is more accurate. Here the rules give $f'(x) = 2x - 3$ for $f(x) = x^2 - 3x$, and the finite difference agrees.

```{python}
def f(x):
    return x**2 - 3 * x


x0, h = 2.5, 1e-6
(f(x0 + h) - f(x0 - h)) / (2 * h), 2 * x0 - 3  # numeric, exact
```

### A loss curve and its tangent

Suppose a one-parameter model $\hat{y} = w x$ fitted to three points. The {{< term mse >}} as a function of $w$ is a curve, and the derivative at any $w$ is the slope of the tangent there.

```{python}
x = np.array([1.0, 2.0, 3.0])
y = np.array([2.0, 4.0, 5.0])


def loss(w):
    return np.mean((y - w * x) ** 2)


w0 = 0.8
slope = (loss(w0 + h) - loss(w0 - h)) / (2 * h)
loss(w0), slope
```

```{python}
#| renderings: [light, dark]
#| fig-alt: "A U-shaped loss curve, mean squared error against the weight w, with a dot on the left arm at w = 0.8 and a dashed tangent line through it sloping steeply downwards to the right. The minimum of the curve is near w = 1.8."
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

ws = np.linspace(0, 3.2, 200)
span = np.linspace(w0 - 0.6, w0 + 0.6, 2)
fig, ax = plt.subplots()
ax.plot(ws, [loss(w) for w in ws], label="loss L(w)")
ax.plot(span, loss(w0) + slope * (span - w0), linestyle="--", label=f"tangent at w = {w0}")
ax.scatter([w0], [loss(w0)], zorder=3)
ax.set(xlabel="weight w", ylabel="mean squared error", title="A 1-D loss curve and its tangent")
ax.legend()
plt.show()
```

At $w = 0.8$ the slope is negative: the loss falls if $w$ increases. At the bottom of the bowl the slope is zero, and to the right it is positive. So the *sign* of the derivative tells you which way to move to reduce the loss, and its *size* tells you how steep the curve is. That is all gradient descent needs, and the boxes below make it precise for many parameters.

### Several parameters: partial derivatives and the gradient

::: {.definition title="Partial derivative and gradient"}
For $L : \mathbb{R}^p \to \mathbb{R}$, the **partial derivative** $\partial L / \partial \theta_j$ at $\theta$ is the ordinary derivative of the one-variable function $t \mapsto L(\theta_1, \ldots, \theta_j + t, \ldots, \theta_p)$ at $t = 0$: all other coordinates are held fixed. The {{< term gradient >}} is the column vector of all partial derivatives,
$$
\nabla L(\theta) = \Big( \frac{\partial L}{\partial \theta_1}, \ldots, \frac{\partial L}{\partial \theta_p} \Big)^{\!\top} \in \mathbb{R}^p .
$$
:::

::: {.theorem title="The gradient is the direction of steepest ascent"}
Let $L$ be differentiable at $\theta$ (it suffices that all partial derivatives exist and are continuous near $\theta$), and let $u \in \mathbb{R}^p$ be a unit vector. The rate of change of $L$ at $\theta$ in the direction $u$ is
$$
\frac{d}{dt} L(\theta + t u) \Big|_{t = 0} = \nabla L(\theta) \cdot u .
$$
If $\nabla L(\theta) \ne 0$, this rate is largest when $u = \nabla L(\theta) / \lVert \nabla L(\theta) \rVert$ and smallest (most negative) when $u = -\nabla L(\theta) / \lVert \nabla L(\theta) \rVert$.
:::

::: {.proof}
The first statement is the multivariable chain rule, which we use without proof: $\frac{d}{dt} L(\theta + tu) = \sum_j \frac{\partial L}{\partial \theta_j} u_j$. For the second, Cauchy–Schwarz gives $|\nabla L \cdot u| \le \lVert \nabla L \rVert \, \lVert u \rVert = \lVert \nabla L \rVert$, with equality exactly when $u$ is a multiple of $\nabla L$; the sign of the multiple decides between the maximum and the minimum.
:::

::: {.theorem title="First-order condition for a minimum"}
If $L$ is differentiable and $\theta^\ast$ is a local minimum of $L$, then $\nabla L(\theta^\ast) = 0$.
:::

::: {.proof}
Fix $j$ and let $g(t) = L(\theta^\ast + t e_j)$, where $e_j$ is the $j$-th standard basis vector. Then $g$ has a local minimum at $t = 0$, so for small $h > 0$ both $(g(h) - g(0))/h \ge 0$ and $(g(-h) - g(0))/(-h) \le 0$. Letting $h \to 0$ gives $g'(0) \ge 0$ and $g'(0) \le 0$, so $\partial L / \partial \theta_j = g'(0) = 0$. As $j$ was arbitrary, the whole gradient vanishes.
:::

The condition is necessary, not sufficient: a maximum or a saddle point also has zero gradient. For the losses of this course a separate argument (like the one for least squares below) shows that the stationary points found are minima.

::: {.definition title="Gradient descent"}
Given a differentiable loss $L$, a starting point $\theta_0$ and a {{< term learning-rate >}} $\eta > 0$, **gradient descent** is the iteration
$$
\theta_{k+1} = \theta_k - \eta\, \nabla L(\theta_k), \qquad k = 0, 1, 2, \ldots
$$
:::

By the steepest-ascent theorem each step moves in the direction in which the loss decreases fastest, and by the first-order condition the iteration stops changing exactly at points where the gradient vanishes, which includes every minimum. Here is the gradient of a two-parameter function at the origin, by finite differences and then by the rules.

```{python}
def g(a, b):
    return (a - 1) ** 2 + 2 * (b + 2) ** 2


grad = np.array([
    (g(0 + h, 0) - g(0 - h, 0)) / (2 * h),  # dg/da at (0, 0)
    (g(0, 0 + h) - g(0, 0 - h)) / (2 * h),  # dg/db at (0, 0)
])
grad.round(4)
```

By the rules, $\partial g/\partial a = 2(a - 1)$ and $\partial g/\partial b = 4(b + 2)$, which at $(0, 0)$ give $(-2, 8)$. Twenty steps of {{< term gradient-descent >}} walk from the origin to within about 0.01 of the minimum at $(1, -2)$, where both partials are zero.

```{python}
theta, eta = np.array([0.0, 0.0]), 0.1
for step in range(20):
    grad = np.array([2 * (theta[0] - 1), 4 * (theta[1] + 2)])
    theta = theta - eta * grad
theta.round(3)
```

### Least squares

The loss of linear regression is simple enough that the minimisers can be described exactly. This is the result that [episode 2.2](../part-1-foundations/ch02-ml-fundamentals/02-linear-regression.html) derives line by line in its deep dive.

::: {.theorem title="Least squares and the normal equations"}
Let $X \in \mathbb{R}^{n \times p}$, $y \in \mathbb{R}^n$, and $L(\theta) = \frac{1}{n} \lVert y - X\theta \rVert^2$. Then

1. $\nabla L(\theta) = -\dfrac{2}{n} X^\top (y - X\theta)$;
2. $\theta$ minimises $L$ if and only if it satisfies the **normal equations** $X^\top X \theta = X^\top y$;
3. if the columns of $X$ are linearly independent, the minimiser is unique and equals $\hat{\theta} = (X^\top X)^{-1} X^\top y$. If they are dependent, the minimisers form a whole affine family $\hat{\theta} + \operatorname{null}(X)$.
:::

::: {.proof}
Item 1: expanding the squared norm with the rules for products, $n L(\theta) = y^\top y - 2\theta^\top X^\top y + \theta^\top X^\top X \theta$. The gradient of $\theta^\top c$ is $c$, and the gradient of $\theta^\top M \theta$ for a symmetric matrix $M$ is $2 M \theta$ (differentiate the double sum $\sum_{i,j} \theta_i M_{ij} \theta_j$ coordinate by coordinate). With $c = X^\top y$ and $M = X^\top X$ this gives $n \nabla L = -2 X^\top y + 2 X^\top X \theta$.

Item 2: a minimiser has zero gradient by the first-order condition, which by item 1 is the normal equations. Conversely, let $\hat{\theta}$ satisfy them and write $r = y - X\hat{\theta}$, so $X^\top r = 0$. For any $v \in \mathbb{R}^p$,
$$
n L(\hat{\theta} + v) = \lVert r - Xv \rVert^2 = \lVert r \rVert^2 - 2\, v^\top X^\top r + \lVert X v \rVert^2 = n L(\hat{\theta}) + \lVert X v \rVert^2 \ge n L(\hat{\theta}),
$$
so $\hat{\theta}$ is a minimiser.

Item 3: the same identity shows that $\hat{\theta} + v$ is also a minimiser exactly when $Xv = 0$. If the columns are independent, $\operatorname{null}(X) = \{0\}$, the minimiser is unique, and by the proposition on $X^\top X$ that matrix is invertible, which gives the formula. (That the normal equations have a solution even when the columns are dependent is true but not proved here.)
:::

::: {.proposition title="Least squares as orthogonal projection"}
$\hat{\theta}$ is a least-squares solution if and only if the residual $y - X\hat{\theta}$ is orthogonal to every column of $X$. Then $X\hat{\theta}$ is the point of the column space $\operatorname{col}(X)$ closest to $y$: the orthogonal projection of $y$ onto $\operatorname{col}(X)$.
:::

::: {.proof}
The $j$-th entry of $X^\top (y - X\hat{\theta})$ is the dot product of column $j$ with the residual, so the normal equations say exactly that the residual is orthogonal to every column. The closest-point statement is the identity in the previous proof read differently: every point of $\operatorname{col}(X)$ is $X(\hat{\theta} + v)$ for some $v$, and its squared distance to $y$ is $\lVert y - X\hat{\theta} \rVert^2 + \lVert Xv \rVert^2$.
:::

In words: the $2$ in the gradient comes from differentiating the square, the minus sign from the inner derivative of $y - X\theta$, and $X^\top$ collects "one dot product per feature" over the residuals. Geometrically, a least-squares fit drops a perpendicular from the vector of measurements onto the space of everything the model can predict. When the columns are dependent (two identical feature columns, or more features than samples) the fit is not unique, which is one of the reasons regularisation exists ([episode 2.4](../part-1-foundations/ch02-ml-fundamentals/04-overfitting-regularisation.html)).

Here is the projection property on real data: body mass regressed on flipper length, with a column of ones for the intercept.

```{python}
Xd = np.column_stack([np.ones(len(penguins)), penguins["flipper_length_mm"]])
yd = penguins["body_mass_g"].to_numpy()
theta_hat = np.linalg.solve(Xd.T @ Xd, Xd.T @ yd)
residual = yd - Xd @ theta_hat
theta_hat.round(2), np.abs(Xd.T @ residual).max(), np.abs(Xd.T @ yd).max()
```

The fit says each extra millimetre of flipper goes with about 50 g of body mass. The residual's dot products with the two columns are zero up to rounding, tiny next to the entries of $X^\top y$ that the solver worked with.

::: {.challenge level=1 title="Check a derivative"}
What is the derivative of $f(x) = 3x^2 + 2x$ at $x = 1$? Confirm with a finite difference.

:::: {.solution}
By the power rule and linearity, $f'(x) = 6x + 2$, so $f'(1) = 8$.

```{python}
def f2(x):
    return 3 * x**2 + 2 * x


(f2(1 + h) - f2(1 - h)) / (2 * h)
```

The numeric value matches to many decimals. If it had not, either the hand derivative or the function would be wrong, which is exactly why this check is worth a line of code whenever you implement a gradient yourself.
::::
:::

::: {.challenge level=1 title="Which way is downhill?"}
For $L(a, b) = a^2 + b^2$, write down the gradient at $(1, 2)$. In which direction does one gradient-descent step move, and where does the method end up?

:::: {.solution}
$\nabla L = (2a, 2b)^\top = (2, 4)^\top$ at $(1, 2)$. A step moves in the direction $-(2, 4)$, that is, towards the origin, and shrinks both coordinates in proportion. Repeated steps with a sensible learning rate converge to $(0, 0)$, the only point where the gradient is zero, and since $L \ge 0 = L(0, 0)$ everywhere it is the minimum.
::::
:::

## Probability

*Used in* [episode 2.3](../part-1-foundations/ch02-ml-fundamentals/03-evaluating-models.html) (why a test score is an estimate), [episode 2.5](../part-1-foundations/ch02-ml-fundamentals/05-classification.html) (probabilities from a classifier, precision and recall) and every chapter that splits data.

### Probability spaces

::: {.definition title="Probability space"}
A **probability space** consists of

1. a **sample space** $\Omega$, the set of possible outcomes of an experiment;
2. a collection of subsets of $\Omega$ called **events**, which contains $\Omega$ and is closed under complements and countable unions;
3. a **probability** $P$ that assigns to each event $A$ a number $P(A)$, such that $P(A) \ge 0$, $P(\Omega) = 1$, and $P(A_1 \cup A_2 \cup \cdots) = P(A_1) + P(A_2) + \cdots$ for every sequence of events that are pairwise **disjoint** (no two can occur together).

The **complement** $A^c$ is the event that $A$ does not occur.
:::

The technical condition on events matters only for continuous outcomes; for everything in this course, any set of outcomes you can describe is an event. The outcome of "pick a compound at random from a library of 10,000" is one compound; the event "it is active" is the set of active compounds; if all compounds are equally likely, its probability is the fraction of actives.

::: {.proposition title="Consequences of the axioms"}
For all events $A$ and $B$:

1. $P(A^c) = 1 - P(A)$, and in particular $P(\emptyset) = 0$;
2. if $A \subseteq B$ then $P(A) \le P(B)$;
3. $P(A \cup B) = P(A) + P(B) - P(A \cap B)$;
4. $P(A \cup B) \le P(A) + P(B)$ (the **union bound**).
:::

::: {.proof}
Item 1: $A$ and $A^c$ are disjoint with union $\Omega$, so $P(A) + P(A^c) = 1$; take $A = \Omega$ for the empty set. Item 2: $B$ is the disjoint union of $A$ and $B \cap A^c$, so $P(B) = P(A) + P(B \cap A^c) \ge P(A)$. Item 3: $A \cup B$ is the disjoint union of $A$ and $B \cap A^c$, and $B$ is the disjoint union of $B \cap A$ and $B \cap A^c$; subtract. Item 4 follows from item 3 because $P(A \cap B) \ge 0$.
:::

::: {.definition title="Conditional probability and independence"}
For events $A, B$ with $P(B) > 0$, the **conditional probability** of $A$ given $B$ is
$$
P(A \mid B) = \frac{P(A \cap B)}{P(B)} .
$$
$A$ and $B$ are **independent** if $P(A \cap B) = P(A)\, P(B)$; when $P(B) > 0$ this is the same as $P(A \mid B) = P(A)$.
:::

::: {.theorem title="Law of total probability"}
If the events $A_1, \ldots, A_k$ are pairwise disjoint, have union $\Omega$ and each has $P(A_i) > 0$, then for every event $B$
$$
P(B) = \sum_{i=1}^{k} P(B \mid A_i)\, P(A_i) .
$$
:::

::: {.proof}
$B$ is the disjoint union of the events $B \cap A_i$, so $P(B) = \sum_i P(B \cap A_i)$, and $P(B \cap A_i) = P(B \mid A_i)\, P(A_i)$ by the definition of conditional probability.
:::

::: {.theorem title="Bayes' theorem"}
For events $A, B$ with $0 < P(A) < 1$ and $P(B) > 0$,
$$
P(A \mid B) = \frac{P(B \mid A)\, P(A)}{P(B)} = \frac{P(B \mid A)\, P(A)}{P(B \mid A)\, P(A) + P(B \mid A^c)\, P(A^c)} .
$$
:::

::: {.proof}
By the definition of conditional probability, $P(A \cap B) = P(A \mid B)\, P(B)$ and also $P(A \cap B) = P(B \mid A)\, P(A)$; equate the two and divide by $P(B)$. The second form expands $P(B)$ with the law of total probability for the two events $A$ and $A^c$, both of positive probability by assumption.
:::

Bayes' theorem is the arithmetic behind every screening result. Take a hypothetical assay for an activity that 2% of a compound library actually has. The assay flags 90% of the truly active compounds (its *sensitivity*, which [episode 2.5](../part-1-foundations/ch02-ml-fundamentals/05-classification.html) calls {{< term recall >}}) and wrongly flags 5% of the inactive ones. A compound comes back flagged: how likely is it to be active? Writing $A$ for "active" and $F$ for "flagged",

$$
P(A \mid F) = \frac{0.9 \times 0.02}{0.9 \times 0.02 + 0.05 \times 0.98} = \frac{0.018}{0.018 + 0.049} \approx 0.27 .
$$

```{python}
prevalence, sensitivity, false_positive_rate = 0.02, 0.90, 0.05
p_flagged = sensitivity * prevalence + false_positive_rate * (1 - prevalence)
posterior = sensitivity * prevalence / p_flagged
round(p_flagged, 3), round(posterior, 3)
```

The assay flags 6.7% of the library, and only about a quarter of the flagged compounds are active, even though the assay is "90% sensitive and 95% specific", because the inactive compounds are so much more numerous that their 5% false positives outnumber the true hits. This quantity, $P(\text{active} \mid \text{flagged})$, is exactly the {{< term precision >}} of a classifier, and the example is why precision collapses on rare classes however good the recall. A simulation with a seeded {{< term rng >}} agrees with the arithmetic.

```{python}
rng = np.random.default_rng(42)
n = 200_000
active = rng.random(n) < prevalence
flagged = np.where(active, rng.random(n) < sensitivity, rng.random(n) < false_positive_rate)
round(active[flagged].mean(), 3)
```

::: {.bridge audience="bio"}
You have met Bayes' theorem whenever a diagnostic test's positive predictive value was quoted next to its sensitivity: the two differ by exactly the base-rate factor above, and a rare condition makes even an excellent test produce mostly false positives. A virtual screen of a library in which 2% of compounds are active is in the same position as a population screen for a rare disease.
:::

### Random variables and their distributions

::: {.definition title="Random variable and distribution function"}
A **random variable** is a function $X : \Omega \to \mathbb{R}$ that assigns a number to each outcome; for every interval $I$, $\{X \in I\}$ is an event. Its **distribution** is the collection of probabilities $P(X \in I)$, and it is summarised by the **(cumulative) distribution function**
$$
F_X(x) = P(X \le x), \qquad x \in \mathbb{R} .
$$
:::

"Pick a compound at random" is the experiment; its molecular weight, its measured logS and the indicator "1 if active, 0 if not" are three random variables on the same sample space.

::: {.definition title="Discrete and continuous random variables"}
$X$ is **discrete** if it takes values in a finite or countable set $\{x_1, x_2, \ldots\}$; its **probability mass function** is $p_X(x_k) = P(X = x_k)$, and $\sum_k p_X(x_k) = 1$. $X$ is **continuous** with **density** $f_X \ge 0$ if
$$
P(a \le X \le b) = \int_a^b f_X(t)\, dt \quad \text{for all } a \le b, \qquad \int_{-\infty}^{\infty} f_X(t)\, dt = 1 .
$$
For a continuous variable every single value has probability zero; only intervals have positive probability.
:::

::: {.proposition title="Properties of distribution functions"}
Every distribution function $F_X$ is non-decreasing, satisfies $F_X(x) \to 0$ as $x \to -\infty$ and $F_X(x) \to 1$ as $x \to \infty$, and gives the probability of an interval: $P(a < X \le b) = F_X(b) - F_X(a)$. If $X$ has density $f_X$, then $F_X(x) = \int_{-\infty}^{x} f_X(t)\, dt$.
:::

::: {.proof}
For $a < b$ the event $\{X \le b\}$ is the disjoint union of $\{X \le a\}$ and $\{a < X \le b\}$, which gives the interval formula and, because probabilities are non-negative, monotonicity. The limits follow from countable additivity applied to the events $\{n - 1 < X \le n\}$, $n \in \mathbb{Z}$, which are disjoint with union $\Omega$. The last statement is the definition of a density with $a \to -\infty$.
:::

### Expectation, variance and covariance

::: {.definition title="Expectation and variance"}
If $X$ is discrete, its **expectation** is $\mathbb{E}[X] = \sum_k x_k\, p_X(x_k)$; if it is continuous, $\mathbb{E}[X] = \int x\, f_X(x)\, dx$ (in both cases provided the sum or integral of $|x|$ is finite). With $\mu = \mathbb{E}[X]$, the **variance** is $\operatorname{Var}(X) = \mathbb{E}\big[(X - \mu)^2\big]$ and the **standard deviation** is $\sigma = \sqrt{\operatorname{Var}(X)}$.
:::

::: {.definition title="Covariance and correlation"}
For random variables $X, Y$ with means $\mu_X, \mu_Y$ and positive standard deviations $\sigma_X, \sigma_Y$, the **covariance** and the **correlation** are
$$
\operatorname{Cov}(X, Y) = \mathbb{E}\big[(X - \mu_X)(Y - \mu_Y)\big], \qquad \rho(X, Y) = \frac{\operatorname{Cov}(X, Y)}{\sigma_X\, \sigma_Y} .
$$
Note that $\operatorname{Cov}(X, X) = \operatorname{Var}(X)$.
:::

::: {.definition title="Independence and i.i.d. samples"}
Random variables $X_1, \ldots, X_n$ are **independent** if $P(X_1 \le x_1, \ldots, X_n \le x_n) = P(X_1 \le x_1) \cdots P(X_n \le x_n)$ for all numbers $x_1, \ldots, x_n$: knowing some of them tells you nothing about the others. They are **independent and identically distributed**, {{< term iid >}}, if in addition they all have the same distribution.
:::

The i.i.d. assumption is the quiet foundation of model evaluation. A random train/test split treats the molecules as i.i.d. draws from one population, so that test molecules behave like the new molecules the model will meet. Duplicates, close analogues of the same compound and batch effects make samples dependent, which is why the test score can then be optimistic, and why Part II replaces random splits with scaffold splits.

::: {.proposition title="Rules for expectation, variance and covariance"}
For random variables $X, Y$ with finite variances and constants $a, b$:

1. $\mathbb{E}[aX + bY] = a\, \mathbb{E}[X] + b\, \mathbb{E}[Y]$ (linearity; no independence needed);
2. $\operatorname{Var}(X) = \mathbb{E}[X^2] - \mu^2$ and $\operatorname{Cov}(X, Y) = \mathbb{E}[XY] - \mu_X \mu_Y$;
3. $\operatorname{Var}(aX + b) = a^2 \operatorname{Var}(X)$;
4. $\operatorname{Var}(X + Y) = \operatorname{Var}(X) + \operatorname{Var}(Y) + 2 \operatorname{Cov}(X, Y)$;
5. if $X$ and $Y$ are independent, then $\mathbb{E}[XY] = \mathbb{E}[X]\, \mathbb{E}[Y]$, so $\operatorname{Cov}(X, Y) = 0$ and $\operatorname{Var}(X + Y) = \operatorname{Var}(X) + \operatorname{Var}(Y)$;
6. $-1 \le \rho(X, Y) \le 1$.
:::

::: {.proof}
Item 1 is the linearity of sums and integrals. Item 2: expand the square or the product inside the expectation and use item 1, for example $\mathbb{E}[(X - \mu)^2] = \mathbb{E}[X^2] - 2\mu\, \mathbb{E}[X] + \mu^2$. Item 3 is the ★★ exercise below. Item 4: expand $\mathbb{E}\big[\big((X - \mu_X) + (Y - \mu_Y)\big)^2\big]$. Item 5: the product rule for independent variables is a standard consequence of the definition (for discrete variables it is $\sum_{j,k} x_j y_k\, p_X(x_j) p_Y(y_k)$, which factorises); the rest follows from items 2 and 4. Item 6 is Cauchy–Schwarz again, applied to $\mathbb{E}[UV]$ with $U = X - \mu_X$, $V = Y - \mu_Y$; the proof is the one given for vectors, with expectations in place of sums.
:::

The converse of item 5 is false: zero covariance does not imply independence. Let $X$ take the values $-1, 0, 1$ with probability $1/3$ each, and let $Y = X^2$. Then $\operatorname{Cov}(X, Y) = \mathbb{E}[X^3] - \mathbb{E}[X]\, \mathbb{E}[X^2] = 0 - 0 = 0$, yet $Y$ is completely determined by $X$. Covariance and correlation only see *linear* association.

```{python}
xs = rng.choice([-1, 0, 1], size=100_000)
ys = xs**2
cov_xy, corr_xy = np.cov(xs, ys)[0, 1], np.corrcoef(xs, ys)[0, 1]
p_y1, p_y1_given_x1 = np.mean(ys == 1), np.mean(ys[xs == 1] == 1)
print(f"Cov {cov_xy:+.4f}   correlation {corr_xy:+.4f}")
print(f"P(Y = 1) = {p_y1:.3f}   but   P(Y = 1 | X = 1) = {p_y1_given_x1:.3f}")
```

The covariance and correlation are zero up to sampling noise, yet learning that $X = 1$ changes the probability of $Y = 1$ from about two thirds to certainty: the variables are as dependent as they could be.

### Four distributions

::: {.definition title="Bernoulli and binomial distributions"}
$X$ is **Bernoulli** with parameter $p \in [0, 1]$ if $P(X = 1) = p$ and $P(X = 0) = 1 - p$. $X$ is **binomial** with parameters $n$ and $p$ if
$$
P(X = k) = \binom{n}{k} p^k (1 - p)^{n - k}, \qquad k = 0, 1, \ldots, n ;
$$
it counts the successes in $n$ independent Bernoulli trials with the same $p$.
:::

::: {.definition title="Uniform and normal distributions"}
$X$ is **uniform** on $[a, b]$ if it has density $1/(b - a)$ on $[a, b]$ and $0$ elsewhere. $X$ is **normal** with mean $\mu$ and variance $\sigma^2 > 0$, written $X \sim N(\mu, \sigma^2)$, if it has the density
$$
f(x) = \frac{1}{\sigma \sqrt{2\pi}} \exp\!\Big( -\frac{(x - \mu)^2}{2\sigma^2} \Big) .
$$
The **standard normal** distribution is $N(0, 1)$; its distribution function is written $\Phi$.
:::

::: {.proposition title="Means and variances of the four distributions"}
| Distribution | $\mathbb{E}[X]$ | $\operatorname{Var}(X)$ |
|---|---|---|
| Bernoulli($p$) | $p$ | $p(1 - p)$ |
| binomial($n$, $p$) | $np$ | $np(1 - p)$ |
| uniform on $[a, b]$ | $(a + b)/2$ | $(b - a)^2 / 12$ |
| $N(\mu, \sigma^2)$ | $\mu$ | $\sigma^2$ |

Moreover, if $X \sim N(\mu, \sigma^2)$ then $(X - \mu)/\sigma \sim N(0, 1)$, so $P(X \le x) = \Phi\big((x - \mu)/\sigma\big)$.
:::

::: {.proof}
Bernoulli: $\mathbb{E}[X] = 0 \cdot (1-p) + 1 \cdot p = p$ and $\mathbb{E}[X^2] = p$, so $\operatorname{Var}(X) = p - p^2$. Binomial: $X = B_1 + \cdots + B_n$ with independent Bernoulli($p$) variables $B_i$, so items 1 and 5 of the rules give $np$ and $np(1 - p)$. Uniform: integrate $x/(b-a)$ and $x^2/(b-a)$ over $[a, b]$. Normal: substituting $z = (x - \mu)/\sigma$ in the integrals turns $N(\mu, \sigma^2)$ into $N(0, 1)$, which proves the last statement; for $N(0, 1)$ the mean is $0$ by symmetry, and the variance, the integral of $z^2$ against the standard normal density, equals $1$ by an integration by parts. The rules for expectation and variance then give $\mu$ and $\sigma^2$.
:::

The Bernoulli variable is the indicator of an event ("this compound is active", "this prediction is correct"); its mean is the probability of the event. A binomial count is how many actives land on a 96-well plate when each well holds an independent compound with a 2% chance of activity:

```{python}
n_wells, p_active = 96, 0.02
plates = rng.binomial(n_wells, p_active, size=100_000)
plates.mean().round(3), plates.var().round(3), n_wells * p_active, round(n_wells * p_active * (1 - p_active), 4)
```

$\Phi$ has no formula in elementary functions, but Python's `math.erf` gives it exactly through $\Phi(z) = \tfrac{1}{2}\big(1 + \operatorname{erf}(z / \sqrt{2})\big)$. The probabilities of landing within one, two and three standard deviations of the mean, used in the next section:

```{python}
from math import erf, sqrt


def Phi(z):
    """Distribution function of the standard normal distribution."""
    return 0.5 * (1 + erf(z / sqrt(2)))


[round(Phi(k) - Phi(-k), 4) for k in (1, 2, 3)]
```

### Averages of many samples

::: {.theorem title="Law of large numbers"}
Let $X_1, X_2, \ldots$ be i.i.d. random variables with mean $\mu$ and finite variance $\sigma^2$, and let $\bar{X}_n = \frac{1}{n}(X_1 + \cdots + X_n)$. Then for every $\varepsilon > 0$,
$$
P\big( |\bar{X}_n - \mu| \ge \varepsilon \big) \le \frac{\sigma^2}{n \varepsilon^2} \longrightarrow 0 \quad \text{as } n \to \infty .
$$
:::

::: {.proof}
By the rules above, $\mathbb{E}[\bar{X}_n] = \mu$ and $\operatorname{Var}(\bar{X}_n) = \sigma^2 / n$. Chebyshev's inequality says that any random variable $Y$ with mean $m$ and variance $v$ satisfies $P(|Y - m| \ge \varepsilon) \le v / \varepsilon^2$; it holds because $(Y - m)^2 \ge \varepsilon^2$ whenever $|Y - m| \ge \varepsilon$, so $v = \mathbb{E}[(Y - m)^2] \ge \varepsilon^2\, P(|Y - m| \ge \varepsilon)$. Apply it to $Y = \bar{X}_n$.
:::

The sample mean of many independent draws settles down to the expectation, and the bound says how fast: the spread of $\bar{X}_n$ shrinks like $\sigma / \sqrt{n}$. Here are the running means of Bernoulli draws with $p = 0.3$, which is also an estimate of a probability by a frequency.

```{python}
#| renderings: [light, dark]
#| fig-alt: "Running mean of Bernoulli draws with p = 0.3 against the number of draws on a logarithmic axis from 1 to 5000, for three independent sequences. All three fluctuate widely for the first few dozen draws and then settle onto the dashed horizontal line at 0.3, with the band of fluctuation narrowing as the number of draws grows."
n_draws = 5000
fig, ax = plt.subplots()
for run in range(3):
    draws = rng.random(n_draws) < 0.3
    ax.plot(np.arange(1, n_draws + 1), np.cumsum(draws) / np.arange(1, n_draws + 1), label=f"sequence {run + 1}")
ax.axhline(0.3, linestyle="--", color="0.3", label="p = 0.3")
ax.set(xscale="log", xlabel="number of draws n", ylabel="running mean", ylim=(0, 1), title="Frequencies converge to probabilities")
ax.legend()
plt.show()
```

The law of large numbers says where the average goes. The next theorem says what its fluctuations look like on the way, whatever the distribution of a single draw.

::: {.theorem title="Central limit theorem"}
Let $X_1, X_2, \ldots$ be i.i.d. with mean $\mu$ and finite variance $\sigma^2 > 0$. Then for every real $z$,
$$
P\Big( \frac{\bar{X}_n - \mu}{\sigma / \sqrt{n}} \le z \Big) \longrightarrow \Phi(z) \quad \text{as } n \to \infty .
$$
In words: for large $n$, $\bar{X}_n$ is approximately $N(\mu, \sigma^2 / n)$.
:::

The proof needs more machinery than this appendix builds (characteristic functions) and is in any probability text. The theorem is easy to watch, though: a single draw from an exponential distribution is strongly skewed, but the standardised mean of 30 such draws is already close to the standard normal curve.

```{python}
#| renderings: [light, dark]
#| fig-alt: "Two histograms side by side. Left: 20,000 single draws from an exponential distribution with mean 1, piled up at zero with a long right tail. Right: the standardised means of 30 draws each, a nearly symmetric bell centred on zero that closely follows the overlaid standard normal density curve."
draws = rng.exponential(scale=1.0, size=(20_000, 30))
z_means = (draws.mean(axis=1) - 1.0) / (1.0 / np.sqrt(30))  # mean 1 and sd 1 for this distribution
z_grid = np.linspace(-4, 4, 200)

fig, (ax1, ax2) = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(9.5, 4))
ax1.hist(draws[:, 0], bins=60, density=True)
ax1.set(title="One draw: skewed", xlabel="value", ylabel="density")
ax2.hist(z_means, bins=60, density=True, label="standardised mean of 30")
ax2.plot(z_grid, np.exp(-z_grid**2 / 2) / np.sqrt(2 * np.pi), label="N(0, 1) density")
ax2.set(title="Mean of 30 draws: close to normal", xlabel="z", ylabel="density")
ax2.legend()
plt.show()
```

Together the two theorems are why every number reported from a {{< term test-set >}} is an *estimate* with a predictable error bar. The accuracy of a classifier on 226 held-out molecules is the sample mean of 226 Bernoulli variables ("prediction $i$ was correct"), so its standard deviation is about $\sqrt{p(1-p)/226}$, roughly 0.03 for $p$ near 0.8, and by the central limit theorem an approximate 95% interval is the accuracy plus or minus twice that, about $\pm 0.05$. Two models whose test accuracies differ by one percentage point are not distinguishable by that test set, whatever the leaderboard says. The same reasoning applies to the MAE and the MSE, which are sample means of per-molecule errors (and so to the RMSE, the square root of the MSE), and it is the reason [episode 2.4](../part-1-foundations/ch02-ml-fundamentals/04-overfitting-regularisation.html) repeats the split with cross-validation.

::: {.challenge level=1 title="A rarer activity"}
Repeat the screening calculation with a prevalence of 0.2% instead of 2%, keeping the sensitivity at 90% and the false-positive rate at 5%. What fraction of flagged compounds are now active? What would the false-positive rate have to fall to for that fraction to reach one half?

:::: {.solution}
With $P(A) = 0.002$: $P(A \mid F) = 0.9 \times 0.002 / (0.9 \times 0.002 + 0.05 \times 0.998) = 0.0018 / 0.0517 \approx 0.035$, about one flagged compound in thirty. For $P(A \mid F) = 0.5$ the two terms in the denominator must be equal: the false-positive rate $r$ must satisfy $r \times 0.998 = 0.0018$, so $r \approx 0.0018$, a false-positive rate of 0.18%, nearly thirty times better than before. Prevalence, not assay quality, is the limiting factor.

```{python}
prev = 0.002
0.9 * prev / (0.9 * prev + 0.05 * (1 - prev)), 0.9 * prev / (1 - prev)
```
::::
:::

::: {.challenge level=1 title="Actives on a plate"}
A 96-well plate holds independent compounds, each active with probability 2%. What are the expected number of actives and its standard deviation? What is the probability that the plate has no active at all?

:::: {.solution}
The count is binomial with $n = 96$ and $p = 0.02$, so its mean is $np = 1.92$ and its standard deviation $\sqrt{np(1-p)} = \sqrt{1.8816} \approx 1.37$. No active means 96 independent failures: $0.98^{96} \approx 0.144$, so about one plate in seven is empty.

```{python}
96 * 0.02, (96 * 0.02 * 0.98) ** 0.5, 0.98**96, (plates == 0).mean()
```

The last number is the fraction of empty plates among the 100,000 simulated above, which agrees.
::::
:::

::: {.challenge level=2 title="Variance of a rescaled variable"}
Prove item 3 of the rules for expectation, variance and covariance: $\operatorname{Var}(aX + b) = a^2 \operatorname{Var}(X)$. Then say in one sentence why standardising a feature (subtracting its mean, dividing by its standard deviation) gives it variance exactly 1, and why for independent $X$ and $Y$ the variance of the *difference* $X - Y$ is $\operatorname{Var}(X) + \operatorname{Var}(Y)$, with a plus sign.

:::: {.solution}
Let $\mu = \mathbb{E}[X]$. By linearity $\mathbb{E}[aX + b] = a\mu + b$, so
$$
\operatorname{Var}(aX + b) = \mathbb{E}\big[(aX + b - a\mu - b)^2\big] = \mathbb{E}\big[a^2 (X - \mu)^2\big] = a^2\, \mathbb{E}\big[(X - \mu)^2\big] = a^2 \operatorname{Var}(X).
$$
Standardising is the case $a = 1/\sigma$, $b = -\mu/\sigma$, so the variance becomes $\sigma^2 / \sigma^2 = 1$ and the shift by $b$ changes nothing. For the difference, $X - Y = X + (-1)Y$, and $-Y$ is independent of $X$ with $\operatorname{Var}(-Y) = (-1)^2 \operatorname{Var}(Y)$: uncertainties add even when the quantities are subtracted, which is why the difference of two noisy measurements is noisier than either.
::::
:::

## Mean, variance and distributions

*Used in* [episode 1.4](../part-1-foundations/ch01-scientific-python/04-visualisation.html), [episode 1.5](../part-1-foundations/ch01-scientific-python/05-eda-solubility.html) (exploring data) and [episode 2.6](../part-1-foundations/ch02-ml-fundamentals/06-pipelines-leakage.html) (standardisation).

The previous section was about random variables, which are idealised objects. This one is about a *list of numbers* you actually have, $x_1, \ldots, x_n$, and the summaries computed from it. The two meet through the law of large numbers: for an i.i.d. sample the quantities below estimate the corresponding expectations.

::: {.definition title="Sample mean, median and variance"}
For numbers $x_1, \ldots, x_n$, the **sample mean**, **sample variance** and **sample standard deviation** are
$$
\bar{x} = \frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^{n} x_i, \qquad s^2 = \frac{1}{n - \text{ddof}}\sum_{i=1}^{n} (x_i - \bar{x})^2, \qquad s = \sqrt{s^2},
$$
where $\text{ddof}$ (delta degrees of freedom) is $0$ or $1$ by convention, see below. The **median** is the middle value of the sorted list, or the mean of the two middle values when $n$ is even.
:::

::: {.theorem title="What the mean and the median minimise"}
For numbers $x_1, \ldots, x_n$:

1. the sample mean is the unique minimiser of $c \mapsto \sum_i (x_i - c)^2$;
2. the median minimises $c \mapsto \sum_i |x_i - c|$ (when $n$ is even, every $c$ between the two middle values does).
:::

::: {.proof}
For item 1, the function $S(c) = \sum_i (x_i - c)^2$ has derivative $S'(c) = -2 \sum_i (x_i - c) = -2(n\bar{x} - nc)$, which vanishes only at $c = \bar{x}$, and $S''(c) = 2n > 0$, so that point is the minimum. For item 2, between consecutive data points the function $\sum_i |x_i - c|$ is linear in $c$ with slope (number of $x_i$ below $c$) minus (number above $c$). The slope is negative while fewer than half the points lie below $c$ and positive once more than half do, so the function decreases until $c$ reaches the median and increases afterwards.
:::

The theorem explains two things used all over the course. The mean is what you get by minimising a *squared* error, which is why the mean is the natural {{< term baseline >}} for a model trained with {{< term mse >}}; and the median is what you get by minimising an *absolute* error, which is why it is robust to a few extreme values (moving one far-away point changes the slope count by one, not the value by a lot).

### Which denominator?

::: {.proposition title="The n − 1 denominator"}
Let $X_1, \ldots, X_n$ be i.i.d. with variance $\sigma^2$, let $\bar{X}$ be their mean, and let $S^2 = \frac{1}{n - 1}\sum_i (X_i - \bar{X})^2$. Then $S^2$ is **unbiased**, $\mathbb{E}[S^2] = \sigma^2$, whereas the version with $n$ in the denominator has expectation $\frac{n-1}{n}\sigma^2$, slightly too small.
:::

::: {.proof}
Write $\mu$ for the common mean. Adding and subtracting $\mu$ inside the square and expanding gives the identity $\sum_i (X_i - \bar{X})^2 = \sum_i (X_i - \mu)^2 - n(\bar{X} - \mu)^2$ (the cross term is $-2(\bar{X} - \mu)\sum_i(X_i - \mu) = -2n(\bar{X} - \mu)^2$). Taking expectations, $\mathbb{E}[(X_i - \mu)^2] = \sigma^2$ for each $i$ and $\mathbb{E}[(\bar{X} - \mu)^2] = \operatorname{Var}(\bar{X}) = \sigma^2 / n$, so the expected sum is $n\sigma^2 - \sigma^2 = (n - 1)\sigma^2$. Dividing by $n - 1$ gives $\sigma^2$; dividing by $n$ gives $\frac{n-1}{n}\sigma^2$.
:::

Libraries disagree about the default, so check rather than assume: draw twenty values from the seeded {{< term rng >}} and ask NumPy and pandas for the standard deviation.

```{python}
sample = rng.normal(loc=10, scale=2, size=20)
np.std(sample), pd.Series(sample).std()
```

```{python}
np.std(sample, ddof=1)  # now equal to the pandas value
```

NumPy uses `ddof=0` and pandas uses `ddof=1`. scikit-learn's `StandardScaler` uses `ddof=0`, like NumPy. With a few hundred samples the difference is well under 1%; what matters is knowing which one a number is before you compare it with another.

### Standardisation: z-scores

::: {.definition title="z-score"}
The **z-score** of a value $x_i$ in a list with mean $\bar{x}$ and standard deviation $s$ is $z_i = (x_i - \bar{x}) / s$. The list $z_1, \ldots, z_n$ has mean $0$ and standard deviation $1$ (with the same $\text{ddof}$ used to compute $s$).
:::

A z-score says how many standard deviations a value sits above (positive) or below (negative) the typical value, whatever the original units; that is what makes features comparable in the distance section above.

```{python}
mass = penguins["body_mass_g"]
z = (mass - mass.mean()) / mass.std()
z.describe().round(2)
```

::: {.bridge audience="bio"}
Expression heatmaps are almost always z-scored gene by gene before plotting. Each row is centred on that gene's own mean and scaled by its own spread, so the colour says "above or below this gene's usual level in this sample", not "high or low counts". Without that step the few highly expressed genes would set the colour scale and everything else would look flat.
:::

### The normal distribution in data

Many measurements, and most noise, pile up around a central value in a symmetric bell shape: the normal distribution of the previous section, fixed entirely by its mean $\mu$ and standard deviation $\sigma$. The central limit theorem is one reason: a quantity built from many small independent contributions tends to be approximately normal.

::: {.proposition title="The 68–95–99.7 rule"}
If $X \sim N(\mu, \sigma^2)$ then, to three decimal places,
$$
P(|X - \mu| \le \sigma) = 0.683, \qquad P(|X - \mu| \le 2\sigma) = 0.954, \qquad P(|X - \mu| \le 3\sigma) = 0.997 .
$$
:::

::: {.proof}
By the standardisation in the proposition on the four distributions, $P(|X - \mu| \le k\sigma) = \Phi(k) - \Phi(-k)$, and the values are those computed with `math.erf` in the probability section: 0.6827, 0.9545 and 0.9973.
:::

A large random sample agrees, to within sampling error (about $\pm 0.003$ for 100,000 draws):

```{python}
big = rng.normal(loc=0, scale=1, size=100_000)
[np.mean(np.abs(big) < k).round(3) for k in (1, 2, 3)]
```

Compare these with the law of large numbers' bound $\sigma^2 / (n\varepsilon^2)$, which for $n = 1$ and $\varepsilon = 2\sigma$ only promises $P(|X - \mu| \ge 2\sigma) \le 1/4$. Chebyshev's inequality holds for *every* distribution and is correspondingly loose; the normal distribution is much more concentrated than the worst case.

Real data is rarely this tidy. Here is the {{< term histogram >}} of penguin body mass with the normal curve of the same mean and standard deviation drawn over it.

```{python}
#| renderings: [light, dark]
#| fig-alt: "A histogram of penguin body mass in grams, from about 2700 to 6300 g, with a smooth bell-shaped normal curve overlaid. The histogram is not a single bell: a tall hump around 3500 g and a lower, broader hump around 5000 g, so the right tail is heavier than the curve predicts."
mu, sigma = mass.mean(), mass.std()
grid = np.linspace(2000, 7000, 300)
normal_pdf = np.exp(-0.5 * ((grid - mu) / sigma) ** 2) / (sigma * np.sqrt(2 * np.pi))

fig, ax = plt.subplots()
ax.hist(mass, bins=25, density=True, alpha=0.6, label="penguins")
ax.plot(grid, normal_pdf, label="normal curve, same mean and sd")
ax.set(xlabel="body mass (g)", ylabel="density", title="Body mass of 333 penguins")
ax.legend()
plt.show()
```

The curve is a poor summary. The data have two humps, Adelie and Chinstrap penguins around 3500 g and the larger Gentoo around 5000 g, so the right tail is heavier than a single bell predicts. With this **skew** the mean (about 4207 g) sits above the median (4050 g): the mean is pulled by every value in the tail, while the median depends only on the order of the values.

```{python}
with_typo = np.append(mass.to_numpy(), 42070.0)  # one mass entered with an extra zero
(mass.mean(), with_typo.mean()), (mass.median(), np.median(with_typo))
```

The mean jumps by over 100 g; the median moves by nothing worth mentioning, as the theorem on what the median minimises predicts. When a quantity is skewed or may contain {{< term outlier plural >}}, report the median alongside the mean, or fix the skew with a logarithm (next section).

### Correlation

::: {.definition title="Pearson correlation"}
For paired numbers $(x_1, y_1), \ldots, (x_n, y_n)$ with z-scores $z^x_i$ and $z^y_i$ (computed with $\text{ddof} = 0$), the **Pearson correlation** is
$$
r = \frac{1}{n} \sum_{i=1}^{n} z^x_i\, z^y_i = \frac{\sum_i (x_i - \bar{x})(y_i - \bar{y})}{\sqrt{\sum_i (x_i - \bar{x})^2}\, \sqrt{\sum_i (y_i - \bar{y})^2}} .
$$
It is the sample version of the correlation $\rho$ of two random variables.
:::

::: {.proposition title="Bounds on the correlation"}
$-1 \le r \le 1$, and $r = \pm 1$ exactly when the points lie on a straight line with positive (respectively negative) slope.
:::

::: {.proof}
The second form of $r$ is the cosine similarity of the two centred vectors $u = (x_i - \bar{x})_i$ and $v = (y_i - \bar{y})_i$, so the Cauchy–Schwarz inequality gives $|r| \le 1$, with equality exactly when $v = \lambda u$ for some scalar $\lambda$, that is when $y_i - \bar{y} = \lambda (x_i - \bar{x})$ for every $i$: a straight line of slope $\lambda$, whose sign is the sign of $r$.
:::

Near $1$ the two variables rise together along a line, near $-1$ one falls as the other rises, near $0$ there is no *linear* relationship. Flipper length and body mass in penguins are strongly correlated.

```{python}
np.corrcoef(penguins["flipper_length_mm"], penguins["body_mass_g"])[0, 1].round(3)
```

Two cautions. {{< term correlation >}} measures straight-line association only: a perfect U-shaped relationship scores close to zero, exactly like the $Y = X^2$ example of the probability section. And it can reverse when groups are mixed: bill length and bill depth are *negatively* correlated across all penguins but *positively* correlated within each species, because the species differ in both. Always look at the scatter plot, coloured by group, before trusting a single $r$.

::: {.challenge level=1 title="Statistics by hand"}
For the values 2, 4, 4, 4, 5, 5, 7, 9, compute the mean, the median, the population variance and standard deviation (`ddof=0`), and the sample standard deviation (`ddof=1`). Check with NumPy and pandas.

:::: {.solution}
Mean $= 40 / 8 = 5$. Median: the sorted middle pair is 4 and 5, so $4.5$. Squared deviations: $9, 1, 1, 1, 0, 0, 4, 16$, summing to $32$. Population variance $= 32/8 = 4$, standard deviation $2$. Sample variance $= 32/7 \approx 4.57$, standard deviation $\approx 2.14$.

```{python}
vals = np.array([2, 4, 4, 4, 5, 5, 7, 9])
vals.mean(), np.median(vals), vals.var(), vals.std(), pd.Series(vals).std()
```
